concepts.name: Constitutional Provisions for Appointment of Supreme Court Judges (Articles 124(2) and 124(3))
key_dimensions: Role of the President, CJI, and consultation vs. concurrence distinction
Eligibility criteria: High Court judge for 5 years OR advocate of High Court for 10 years OR distinguished jurist — only the last is NOT a constitutional post requirement
UPSC trap: 'Consultation' with CJI is mandatory but not binding — pre-collegium era vs. post-collegium binding nature
Distinction between appointment of CJI vs. other SC judges in terms of who is consulted

concepts.name: Evolution of the Collegium System: Three Judges Cases
key_dimensions: First Judges Case (S.P. Gupta, 1981): Executive primacy — CJI's opinion not binding
Second Judges Case (Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record, 1993): Judicial primacy — CJI's collegium opinion binding
Third Judges Case (Presidential Reference, 1998): Collegium expanded to CJI + 4 senior-most judges; definition of 'consultation' as 'concurrence'
UPSC trap: Collegium has NO constitutional basis — it is entirely judge-made law through interpretation of Article 124(2)

concepts.name: National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) — 99th Constitutional Amendment and its Striking Down
key_dimensions: NJAC composition: CJI + 2 senior SC judges + Law Minister + 2 eminent persons (selected by PM, CJI, LoP)
Supreme Court struck it down in 2015 (Fourth Judges Case / NJAC Case) — violation of basic structure (judicial independence)
UPSC trap: The 99th Amendment inserted Article 124A, 124B, 124C and amended Article 127, 128, 217, 222, 224, 224A, 231
Majority (4:1) held NJAC unconstitutional; Justice Chelameswar's dissent — key angle for essay/mains

concepts.name: Appointment of Chief Justice of India — Convention vs. Constitutional Provision
key_dimensions: Article 124(2) gives President discretion, but constitutional convention: senior-most SC judge is appointed CJI
Supersession controversy of 1973 (A.N. Ray) and 1977 (M.H. Beg) — political interference angle
Post-1993: Convention has hardened into a near-binding norm reinforced by collegium system
UPSC trap: Constitution does NOT explicitly mandate seniority for CJI appointment — it is a convention, not a legal requirement

concepts.name: Appointment of High Court Judges — Article 217 and Consultative Process
key_dimensions: President consults CJI, Governor of the state, AND Chief Justice of the concerned High Court — all three mandatory
UPSC trap: For SC judges, Governor is NOT consulted; for HC judges, Governor IS consulted — common confusion point
Eligibility: Citizen of India + HC advocate for 10 years OR judicial office holder for 10 years (no 'distinguished jurist' category for HC)
Collegium for HC appointments: CJI + 2 senior-most SC judges (smaller than SC appointment collegium)

concepts.name: Transfer of High Court Judges — Article 222 and Judicial Independence Concerns
key_dimensions: President can transfer a HC judge after consultation with CJI — CJI's opinion is binding post-Second Judges Case
Chief Justice of a HC can also be transferred under Article 222
UPSC trap: Transfer of HC judges does NOT require consent of the judge being transferred or the Governor
S.P. Gupta case held transfers valid; post-1993, CJI collegium's concurrence is the real check

concepts.name: Removal of Supreme Court Judges — Impeachment Process under Article 124(4)
key_dimensions: Grounds: Proved misbehaviour OR incapacity — both are required to be 'proved' (not merely alleged)
Process: Address by each House of Parliament with Special Majority (majority of total membership + 2/3 of members present and voting)
Judges Inquiry Act, 1968: Three-member committee (SC judge + HC CJ + distinguished jurist) investigates before address is moved
UPSC trap: No SC judge has ever been successfully impeached — Justice V. Ramaswami motion failed in 1993 (Congress abstained); Justice Dipak Misra notice in 2018 rejected by RS Chairman

concepts.name: Removal of High Court Judges — Article 217(1)(b) and Comparison with SC Judges
key_dimensions: Same impeachment procedure as SC judges under Article 124(4) applies to HC judges via Article 218
UPSC trap: Article 218 explicitly makes Articles 124(4) and 124(5) applicable to HCs — procedure is IDENTICAL
HC judges can also cease to hold office if appointed as SC judge or transferred — not a removal but vacation of office
Distinction: HC judge's appointment involves more consultees than SC judge's, but removal procedure is the same

concepts.name: Special Majority Requirement for Impeachment — Constitutional Nuances
key_dimensions: Requires majority of total membership of each House AND 2/3rd majority of members present and voting — BOTH conditions must be met simultaneously
UPSC trap: This is a higher threshold than ordinary special majority (which only requires 2/3rd present and voting) — it combines absolute + qualified majority
Both Houses must pass the address in the SAME SESSION
Comparison with removal of other constitutional functionaries: Same process for CAG, Election Commissioners (after 2023 amendment) — but different from removal of Vice President or President

concepts.name: Acting Chief Justice of India and Ad Hoc Judges — Articles 126 and 127
key_dimensions: Article 126: President appoints acting CJI when CJI office is vacant or CJI is unable to perform duties — President's discretion, no consultation mandated
Article 127: President can appoint ad hoc judges of SC with consent of CJI and the HC Chief Justice concerned — HC judge temporarily sits in SC
UPSC trap: Ad hoc judges are HC judges, NOT retired SC judges — retired SC judges are covered under Article 128
Article 128: Retired SC judges can be requested by CJI (with President's prior consent) to sit and act — they are not 'appointed' but 'requested'

concepts.name: Acting Chief Justice of High Court and Additional/Acting HC Judges — Articles 223 and 224
key_dimensions: Article 223: Governor appoints acting CJ of HC when office is vacant or CJ is unable to perform duties
Article 224: President can appoint additional HC judges (for temporary work increase) for up to 2 years, and acting judges when a permanent judge is temporarily absent
UPSC trap: Article 224A provides for appointment of retired HC judges — requires consent of the retired judge AND the President; initiated by HC Chief Justice
Distinction between 'additional judge' (new workload), 'acting judge' (substitute for existing judge), and 'retired judge' under 224A

concepts.name: Security of Tenure and Service Conditions of SC and HC Judges — Constitutional Safeguards
key_dimensions: SC judges hold office till age 65; HC judges till age 62 — UPSC commonly tests this distinction
Salaries charged to Consolidated Fund of India (SC) and Consolidated Fund of the State (HC) — not votable, ensuring independence
UPSC trap: After appointment, SC judge's service conditions cannot be varied to their disadvantage — but Parliament can change conditions prospectively
SC judges cannot practice in any court after retirement; HC judges cannot practice in the HC where they were judge — different restrictions

concepts.name: Memorandum of Procedure (MoP) for Judicial Appointments — Executive-Judiciary Standoff
key_dimensions: MoP governs the collegium process — currently being renegotiated between government and judiciary since 2016 (post-NJAC verdict)
Government can return a collegium recommendation but must accept if collegium reiterates — government's only tool is delay
UPSC trap: MoP has no statutory or constitutional backing — it is an executive-judiciary administrative arrangement
Recent controversy: Government sitting on collegium recommendations for months/years — judicial criticism of 'pocket veto' by executive

concepts.name: Judicial Independence vs. Judicial Accountability — The Core Tension in Appointment Debates
key_dimensions: Arguments for collegium: Insulates judiciary from executive interference, protects basic structure doctrine
Arguments against collegium: Opaque, nepotism concerns, no accountability mechanism, 'judges appointing judges'
Second Administrative Reforms Commission and Law Commission recommendations for independent commission
Comparative angle: UK's Judicial Appointments Commission, USA's Senate confirmation — UPSC essay/mains relevance

concepts.name: Eligibility Criteria Comparison: SC vs. HC Judges — Constitutional Provisions
key_dimensions: SC judge eligibility (Article 124(3)): HC judge for 5 years OR HC advocate for 10 years OR distinguished jurist in President's opinion
HC judge eligibility (Article 217(2)): Judicial office in India for 10 years OR HC advocate for 10 years — NO 'distinguished jurist' category
UPSC trap: 'Distinguished jurist' category exists ONLY for SC, not HC — and has never been used in practice
Both require citizenship of India; no minimum age prescribed constitutionally (unlike many other countries)

concepts.name: Oath of SC and HC Judges — Articles 124(6) and 219
key_dimensions: SC judges take oath before the President; HC judges take oath before the Governor of the state
Oath content: To bear true faith and allegiance to Constitution, uphold sovereignty and integrity, perform duties without fear or favour, and uphold the Constitution and laws
UPSC trap: Third schedule prescribes the form of oath — judges swear to 'uphold the Constitution' (unlike MPs who swear to 'bear true faith and allegiance')
CJI administers oath to other SC judges; the distinction of who administers oath to CJI (President does directly)

concepts.name: Transparency and Disclosure in Collegium Recommendations — Recent Developments
key_dimensions: 2017 onwards: Supreme Court collegium began publishing reasons for recommendations and transfers on SC website — landmark transparency step
RTI applicability to CJI's office: SC held in 2019 that CJI's office is a 'public authority' under RTI Act
UPSC trap: Publishing reasons is a collegium self-imposed practice, NOT a constitutional or statutory requirement
Tension between judicial privacy (in personal matters) and public accountability in appointments — relevant for ethics paper

concepts.name: Removal of CJI vs. Other SC Judges — Procedural Distinction and In-House Procedure
key_dimensions: Constitutionally, removal procedure is identical for CJI and other SC judges under Article 124(4)
In-House Procedure (1999): SC developed internal mechanism for inquiring into misconduct of judges short of impeachment — CJI can request voluntary resignation
UPSC trap: In-House Procedure has no statutory basis and is not legally enforceable — judge can refuse to resign
Justice Soumitra Sen case (2011): First HC judge to be impeached by Rajya Sabha but resigned before Lok Sabha vote — procedural nuance

concepts.name: Appointment of Lok Adalat, Tribunal, and Other Quasi-Judicial Bodies — Distinction from Constitutional Courts
key_dimensions: Tribunal judges/members are NOT appointed through collegium — executive appoints them (subject to service conditions set by Parliament)
Rojer Mathew case (2019) and Madras Bar Association cases: SC held that tribunal appointments must be insulated from executive control
UPSC trap: 'Judicial independence' doctrine applies to constitutional courts (SC, HC) — its application to tribunals is evolving and contested
Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021: Reduced tenure and changed search committee composition — SC struck down some provisions as violating separation of powers

concepts.name: Collegium System and Representation Concerns — Diversity in Judicial Appointments
key_dimensions: Criticism: Collegium appointments lack diversity — underrepresentation of women, SC/ST communities, and minority communities
Constitutional silence: Article 124 does not mandate any reservation or diversity criteria in judicial appointments
UPSC trap: There is NO constitutional provision for reservation in judiciary — any diversity is at collegium's discretion
Recent data points: First woman SC judge (M. Fathima Beevi, 1989); first woman CJI — yet to happen; diversity debate relevant for GS2 governance questions
